title: The world Church
hook: the Catholic Church's center of gravity shifts toward Latin America, Africa and Asia

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jubilee of Hope: pilgrims on the long avenue to Saint Peter's, and a holy door opened inside a prison. Your line was pilgrims of hope. What did you set down when you arrived? Day nine hundred forty-two.

Some Sunday mornings now look like this. In a small town in the American Midwest, the priest at the altar grew up in Nigeria. In a parish in Ireland, the homily comes in the accent of southern India. In Kinshasa, a choir comes up the aisle dancing, with drums. In Manila, the doors are open because the crowd won't fit inside. And in Rome, the last two popes came from Buenos Aires and from a missionary life in Peru. Same Mass, same prayers, many languages. Today is about where the Catholic Church lives now.
screen: `A NIGERIAN PRIEST IN THE MIDWEST.` → `DRUMS IN KINSHASA.` → `POPES FROM THE AMERICAS.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. The Creed at Mass calls the Church catholic, and the Catechism says plainly what that means: universal. A church for everyone, everywhere. For long stretches of history, though, the center of Catholic life sat in Europe: its bishops, its universities, the missionaries it sent out. That picture has changed. Writers who follow the Church describe its center of gravity moving south, toward Latin America, Africa and Asia, and they point to the Church's own yearly statistics to show it. You can see it at a great Mass in Rome now, in the languages of the readings and in the faces of the newest cardinals. Catholics read their oldest texts as pointing this way from the start. At the end of Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sends the apostles out: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations." And at Pentecost, in Acts, the crowd in Jerusalem is Jews gathered from far and wide, "devout men, out of every nation under heaven," each hearing the apostles speak in his own language. Some readers call Pentecost the Church's birthday, and notice that on its first day it already spoke more than one language. The shift isn't a tidy story. In some places the faith arrived with missionaries who traveled alongside colonial powers, and that history includes real harm, which the Church has had to face. But the faith also spread through local catechists, mothers and grandmothers, and converts who made it their own and sang it to their own music. Today the traffic runs in every direction: African and Asian priests serve European parishes, Latin American theologians are read in seminaries far away, and bishops from every continent sit together at synods in Rome. The church moved south. It also kept moving.
screen: `CATHOLIC: UNIVERSAL.` · `A CENTER OF GRAVITY MOVING SOUTH.` · `EVERY NATION UNDER HEAVEN.` · `TRAFFIC IN EVERY DIRECTION.` · then, large: `GOING THEREFORE, TEACH YE ALL NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for the Church in Africa. Settle, and breathe. Africa is a whole continent, not one place, so let one face or one city come to mind: a priest you've met, a choir you've heard, a country you know only by its name on a map. Hold it there. Now picture a parish somewhere on that continent getting ready for Sunday. Someone sweeping the floor. Someone tuning a drum. A catechist walking in from a village. If you pray, you can pray for that parish and its people. If you don't, simply wish them well, by name if you have one. The bell holds the time.
The world Church. The Catholic Church as it is now: on every continent, with its center of gravity moving toward Latin America, Africa and Asia.
Your line: the church moved south. Today, learn one thing about the Catholic Church in a country you've never visited: a saint, a song, a bishop, a feast. Day nine hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the same Mass in many languages and musical styles, and some parishes in Europe and North America are served by priests and religious sisters from Africa, Asia and Latin America.
